FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond

Bingjun Luo Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Beijing, China Email: bingjunluo@outlook.com    Jialin Guo Affiliation: Harbin Engineering University Affiliation: Harbin, China Email: guojialin@hrbeu.edu.cn    Siqi Li ††thanks: Corresponding author: Siqi Li (lisiqi19971013@gmail.com). Affiliation: BNRist, THUIBCS, School of Software Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Beijing, China Email: lisiqi19971013@gmail.com
Abstract

Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.

1 Introduction

Long-video question answering has become a stress test for multimodal models: the system must search, aggregate, and reason over visual evidence spread across minutes or hours of video. Recent benchmarks such as Video-MME-v2, MLVU, and LongVideoBench make this pressure explicit by evaluating models across long durations, diverse domains, subtitles, and multi-step question groups (Fu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024). Because compute and context length restrict the number of frames that current video–language models can ingest, frame budget has become a central evaluation knob. The de facto protocol is to fix a uniform per-question budget and apply it to every instance. This is simple and reproducible, but it tacitly assumes that every question deserves the same amount of visual evidence.

That assumption sits uneasily with the structure of modern long-video benchmarks. Their questions span heterogeneous evidence demands: some are resolvable from sparse global context, scene-level commonsense, or subtitle cues, while others hinge on local visual details, long-range temporal association, action ordering, or repeated-action counting. Spending the same number of frames on every question therefore creates two coupled inefficiencies: low-demand questions consume frames they may not need, and high-demand questions remain under-observed. Recent efficient video-QA work makes a related observation, showing that uniformly sampled long videos contain substantial redundancy and that question-aware frame selection can recover crucial spatiotemporal cues (Park et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Ben-Ami et al., 2026). Our focus is orthogonal to which frames a question keeps: we ask how much evidence each question should receive under the same average cost.

Our diagnostic analysis on Video-MME-v2 reinforces this view. Within a frozen bank of low-, mid-, and high-budget full-video uniform policies, neighboring budgets repair a non-trivial slice of mid-budget errors while also breaking questions that the mid-budget policy answers correctly. The three policies do not form nested error sets; their disagreement varies systematically with question group and difficulty. This motivates fixed-mean frame-budget routing: given a uniform reference budget BrefB_{\mathrm{ref}} over NN questions, an admissible router may assign per-question budgets BiB_{i} subject to 1N​∑i=1NBi=Bref\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}B_{i}=B_{\mathrm{ref}}. Under this strict equality, any gain must come from reallocating visual evidence across questions, not from increasing the average number of frames. This framing is complementary to query-aware frame selectors and to architecture-level token compressors, which adapt what or how to sample within a fixed per-question quota; here, we ask how the dataset-level budget itself should be distributed.

We instantiate this formulation as FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that routes frame budgets, not frame locations. FrameRouter scores the benchmark question prompt, whose multiple-choice options are visible to any evaluated system, and uses those question-only priorities to choose among frozen low-, mid-, and high-budget full-video policies under an exact dataset-level mean-budget constraint. The router never sees the video, subtitles, sibling questions, other videos, labels, or candidate policy outputs, and it neither fine-tunes the underlying VLM nor introduces a new within-question frame selector. This keeps the comparison tightly controlled: low- and high-budget assignments change the distribution of visual evidence across questions, while the average number of frames remains identical to the uniform reference. Across Video-MME-v2, LongVideoBench, MVBench, and VideoMMMU, FrameRouter yields stable matched-budget improvements. Quota sweeps and post-hoc route audits further show that the benefit is not simply a high-budget effect, but comes from reallocating the fixed average budget across heterogeneous questions.

In summary, our contributions are threefold as follows:

  • •

    We diagnose non-monotonic frame-budget effects on Video-MME-v2 and formalize fixed-mean frame-budget routing as a controlled inference problem, separating dataset-level budget reallocation from variable-frame efficiency and from within-question frame selection.

  • •

    We instantiate this problem as FrameRouter, combining a frozen full-video uniform policy bank, a question-only evidence-demand priority parser, and a quota-constrained allocator that holds the mean frame budget exactly equal to the uniform reference.

  • •

    We achieve the state-of-the-art open-source result on Video-MME-v2 under the matched-budget protocol, and show consistent improvements across other benchmarks, including LongVideoBench, MVBench, and VideoMMMU.

2 Related work

2.1 Long-video understanding benchmarks

Long-video understanding has moved from short, isolated clips toward benchmarks that require models to integrate evidence over minutes or hours. EgoSchema introduced a diagnostic multiple-choice setting over three-minute egocentric clips, emphasizing that temporal difficulty is not captured by clip length alone (Mangalam et al., 2023). Video-MME broadened evaluation across video duration, domain, and modality, including subtitles and audio, and exposed a large gap between frontier proprietary systems and open models on long-video analysis (Fu et al., 2025). MLVU and LongVideoBench further expanded the evaluation surface with multi-task long-video understanding and interleaved video-language contexts (Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024). These benchmarks made frame budget a practical evaluation variable: model quality depends not only on the backbone, but also on how many frames or visual tokens are admitted into the context.

Video-MME-v2 sharpens this pressure by changing both the data distribution and the scoring rule (Fu et al., 2026). It contains 800 recent videos and 3,200 questions, organized into groups of four interrelated questions. Beyond average per-question accuracy, the benchmark reports group-level non-linear scores, including Non-Lin, Consistency, and Coherence, that reward models for answering related questions consistently and for preserving multi-step reasoning chains within a group. These metrics matter for budgeted inference because the same video can contain questions with very different evidence demands: global story context, long-range temporal aggregation, local perceptual details, OCR, or screen evidence. A uniform frame budget is therefore poorly matched to the heterogeneity that Video-MME-v2 is well suited to surfacing.

2.2 Efficient video question answering

The high cost of video QA has motivated methods that reduce redundant visual processing. Early long-video QA systems often uniformly sampled many frames and converted them into captions or visual tokens, but long videos contain large regions that are irrelevant to a particular question. As models and benchmarks move to longer inputs, evaluation quality depends not only on the VLM backbone but also on frame budget, sampling density, and whether auxiliary channels such as subtitles or interleaved text are admitted into the context. The official 64-frame-with-subtitle setting in Video-MME-v2 makes this cost–accuracy tradeoff explicit: more evidence can help difficult questions, but increasing the per-question budget uniformly also spends frames on questions that may not need them.

Existing efficient video-QA methods mostly reduce the cost of processing each question. LVNet explicitly argues that many sampled frames are unnecessary and uses a hierarchical keyframe selector to reduce the captioning burden for long-form QA (Park et al., 2026). Agentic approaches such as VideoAgent ask an LLM controller to iteratively search for useful visual information under a limited frame budget (Wang et al., 2024). Architecture-level approaches also attack the cost problem by compressing the video representation: MA-LMM maintains a memory bank for long-term video information (He et al., 2024), while LongVU uses spatiotemporal adaptive compression to reduce token redundancy while preserving salient visual detail (Shen et al., 2024). These works establish that long-video QA is governed by a cost–accuracy tradeoff, but their primary unit of adaptation is usually the video, the segment, or the selected frame set for a single query.

2.3 Adaptive visual evidence and test-time compute

Most recent efficient video-LLM methods adapt which visual evidence is shown to the model, while a broader adaptive-compute literature studies inference-time allocation more generally. Query-aware frame selection methods score frames by their relevance to the current question, often combining temporal coverage with visual-textual matching. Q-Frame selects frames and adapts resolution according to the video content and query (Zhang et al., 2025); GenS trains a generative frame sampler under capped frame budgets (Yao et al., 2025); and HiMu composes expert grounding signals for hierarchical frame selection (Ben-Ami et al., 2026). In language-model serving and conditional computation, FrugalGPT uses query-dependent cascades to reduce cost (Chen et al., 2023), RouteLLM routes between stronger and weaker LLMs as a cost-quality tradeoff (Ong et al., 2024), and Mixture-of-Depths allocates transformer computation dynamically across tokens (Raposo et al., 2024). Input-dependent mixture-of-experts routing has likewise been adopted beyond language modeling (Xi et al., 2025). These works share the premise that uniform computation is wasteful when inputs have heterogeneous difficulty.

Our work connects these two perspectives in long-video QA. Rather than learning a new retriever, selecting timestamps, or routing between different models, FrameRouter reallocates a fixed dataset-level frame budget across questions using frozen VLM inference configurations. Thus it is complementary to within-question frame selection: those methods ask which evidence to keep, whereas we ask how much visual evidence each question should receive under the same average budget.

3 Analysis: why route frame budgets?

We argue that uniform frame budgets are a poor unit of comparison on Video-MME-v2, and that the right unit is a per-question budget assignment chosen under a dataset-level mean-frame constraint. To make this argument without conflating budget allocation with other design choices, we analyze a frozen policy bank of three full-video uniform sampling policies: low, mid, and high budget, instantiated as 48, 64, and 96 frames. The policies use the same video–language model, prompt, subtitles setting, and full-video uniform sampler, differing only in the number of sampled frames. We use this bank only as a diagnostic object: it lets us ask whether errors made by the mid-budget reference are sometimes recoverable by neighboring budgets, and whether such recovery has structure across question types. Any routed policy is compared to the uniform reference under the same dataset-level mean frame budget; the formal budget constraint is introduced in Section 4. Figure 2 evaluates the question-level headroom and structure of this bank in the main Think-with-subtitles setting on the Video-MME-v2 full set.

3.1 Mid-budget error recovery

Figure 2(a) first asks whether the standard mid-budget policy is merely making irrecoverable errors, or whether some of its errors are artifacts of choosing one uniform budget for every question. We use the mid policy as the reference and inspect only its errors. This is an oracle diagnostic over the frozen policy bank: it is not available to the deployed router, but it measures the headroom available to a question-conditioned budget selector restricted to the same bank.

The recoverable errors are split almost evenly between the two neighboring budgets: low-only and high-only recovery occupy similar shares, with a smaller overlap recovered by both neighboring policies. Thus the headroom is not only a high-budget effect. Increasing the budget can also hurt: the high policy introduces its own errors on cases that the mid policy answers correctly. The frozen bank therefore does not define a nested error set in which more frames are uniformly better. Instead, it defines an allocation problem: under the same mid-budget mean, can we promote the questions that need denser coverage while compressing questions whose evidence is already sufficiently localized?

3.2 Question-level disagreement

We next ask where this non-nested behavior concentrates. If disagreement were uniformly scattered across the benchmark, a question-conditioned router would have little structure to exploit. Instead, the correction patterns vary with observable question groups and difficulty levels.

Figure 2(b) shows that this disagreement changes with both question group and difficulty level. We split the questions with official group and level labels by (group_type,level)(\texttt{group\_type},\texttt{level}) and plot a small pairwise correction matrix for each split: each entry is the percentage of questions in that split for which the row budget is correct and the column budget is wrong.

This pattern indicates that the three uniform policies do not form nested error sets: they make systematically different mistakes at the question level. We use this disagreement only as evidence that budget heterogeneity exists. A deployable route must infer budget demand before answering, from the current question and options alone.

3.3 From diagnostics to design

These diagnostics suggest a narrow design space for a deployable router. To isolate budget allocation from frame-selection effects, the route should choose among the frozen full-video policies in Π\Pi rather than introduce a new sampler or temporal localizer. To avoid test-time leakage, the routing signal should be computed from the current question prompt only, excluding labels, videos, subtitles, sibling questions, other videos, model answers, and policy outcomes. Because the route cannot observe which policy will be correct, the signal should be an interpretable prior over evidence demand rather than a direct correctness predictor. Finally, comparisons must enforce the same dataset-level mean frame budget as the uniform reference; higher means are separate operating points.

4 FrameRouter

FrameRouter turns the question-level budget disagreement in Section 3 into a deployable routing method: it estimates question-side evidence demand, routes each question to one frozen full-video uniform policy, and enforces an exact mean-frame budget. It routes frame budgets, not frame locations, and never modifies the underlying video–language model.

4.1 Problem formulation

Let 𝒟={(vi,qi,si,yi)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(v_{i},q_{i},s_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a video question-answering dataset, where viv_{i} is a video, qiq_{i} is the complete question prompt including the answer options, sis_{i} is any auxiliary textual context associated with the question (e.g., subtitles when provided by the benchmark), and yiy_{i} is the ground-truth answer. The auxiliary context sis_{i} may be used by the answer model, but it is not used as a routing signal. The downstream task is multiple-choice video question answering: produce a prediction y^i\hat{y}_{i} for each instance ii. We treat the number of video frames spent on instance ii as a problem-level variable Bi∈ℕB_{i}\in\mathbb{N}, abstracting away the mechanism that produces those frames. A frame-budgeted predictor is any procedure that, given BiB_{i} frames of viv_{i} together with (qi,si)(q_{i},s_{i}), returns an answer

y^i=F⁡(vi,qi,si,Bi).\hat{y}_{i}\;=\;F\!\left(v_{i},\,q_{i},\,s_{i};\,B_{i}\right). (1)

To make accuracy comparisons faithful to a fixed compute envelope, any solution must spend, on average, exactly BrefB_{\mathrm{ref}} frames per question. We denote the corresponding uniform reference policy by πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and require 1N​∑i=1NBi=Bref\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}B_{i}=B_{\mathrm{ref}}. Operating points that under- or over-spend this reference are different points on the cost–accuracy plane and must be reported separately. FrameRouter is a practical approximation to this fixed-budget assignment problem: each parser call is question-only, and the solver uses only parser scores and route quotas rather than labels or policy outcomes.

4.2 Method overview

FrameRouter instantiates the fixed-mean budget assignment problem with a method-specific frozen policy bank

Π={πlow,πmid,πhigh},\Pi\;=\;\{\pi_{\mathrm{low}},\,\pi_{\mathrm{mid}},\,\pi_{\mathrm{high}}\}, (2)

where each policy uniformly samples from the full video and uses the same frozen video–language model and prompting protocol. The policies differ only in their frame budgets, with Blow<Bmid<BhighB_{\mathrm{low}}<B_{\mathrm{mid}}<B_{\mathrm{high}}. FrameRouter does not modify the policy bank, the sampler, or the underlying model; it only decides which bank member to use for each question.

The routing pipeline has two stages. First, an evidence-demand priority parser assigns each instance two priorities: whether it is safe to compress to the low-budget policy, and whether it is worth promoting to the high-budget policy. Second, a quota-constrained allocator converts these priorities into routes over Π\Pi while preserving the same dataset-level mean frame budget as the uniform reference. At inference time, FrameRouter executes only the selected policy for each question; the other bank policies are not run, so the method performs budget routing rather than late selection over candidate answers.

4.3 Evidence-demand priority parser

The analysis in Section 3 shows that budget effects vary across questions rather than following a simple high-budget-fixes-low-budget pattern. Because group labels, videos, subtitles, and policy outcomes are not available to a deployed router, FrameRouter estimates evidence demand from the question prompt itself. To keep this signal interpretable and auditable, it does not directly predict which policy will answer correctly. Instead, a frozen text-only parser assigns two priorities to the current question:

gϕ​(qi)=(pilow,pihigh),g_{\phi}(q_{i})\;=\;\left(p_{i}^{\mathrm{low}},\,p_{i}^{\mathrm{high}}\right), (3)

where pilow,pihigh∈[0,1]p_{i}^{\mathrm{low}},p_{i}^{\mathrm{high}}\in[0,1] are direction-specific scores rather than a normalized distribution. The low-priority score estimates how safe it is to compress instance ii to the low-budget policy, for example when the answer appears anchored to local, static, single-moment, or explicit textual evidence. The high-priority score estimates how useful additional coverage may be, for example for counting, ordering, change tracking, broad temporal evidence, or fine visual discrimination across moments. For auditing, the same parser also returns auxiliary fields such as confidence, evidence-anchor category, optional route suggestion, and a short rationale; these fields are not consumed by the allocator.

The parser prompt and underlying LLM checkpoint, denoted by ϕ\phi, are fixed before evaluation and are never updated using benchmark labels, policy outcomes, or category-level performance. The parser uses deterministic decoding and sees only qiq_{i}, including the multiple-choice options that are part of the task input. It does not see the video, subtitles, sibling questions, other videos, the correct answer label, or any candidate answers generated by the policy bank. Thus the priority pair is a question-only prior over evidence demand, not a temporal localization claim: FrameRouter never predicts timestamps, and all policies in Π\Pi remain full-video uniform samplers.

4.4 Quota-constrained allocation

Given the priority scores produced by gϕg_{\phi} in Eq. (3), FrameRouter must turn them into routes {ri}i=1N\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} that satisfy the dataset-level mean-budget constraint 1N​∑i=1NBri=Bref\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}B_{r_{i}}=B_{\mathrm{ref}} exactly. We do this through a quota-constrained allocator that decouples how many questions are sent to each policy from which questions are sent there. The first choice is fixed by an operating-point quota under the budget constraint; the second is determined by two priority rankings.

Quota selection.

Let nlow,nmid,nhigh∈ℤ≥0n_{\mathrm{low}},n_{\mathrm{mid}},n_{\mathrm{high}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} denote the number of instances assigned to each policy in Π\Pi. For a chosen operating point, FrameRouter fixes a feasible quota triple with nlow+nmid+nhigh=Nn_{\mathrm{low}}+n_{\mathrm{mid}}+n_{\mathrm{high}}=N and (Blow​nlow+Bmid​nmid+Bhigh​nhigh)/N=Bref(B_{\mathrm{low}}n_{\mathrm{low}}+B_{\mathrm{mid}}n_{\mathrm{mid}}+B_{\mathrm{high}}n_{\mathrm{high}})/N=B_{\mathrm{ref}}. This encodes the mean-budget constraint exactly at the dataset level rather than only in expectation. Specializing to the common setting Bref=BmidB_{\mathrm{ref}}=B_{\mathrm{mid}}, this condition is equivalently

(Bmid−Blow)​nlow=(Bhigh−Bmid)​nhigh,(B_{\mathrm{mid}}-B_{\mathrm{low}})n_{\mathrm{low}}=(B_{\mathrm{high}}-B_{\mathrm{mid}})n_{\mathrm{high}}, (4)

with nmid=N−nlow−nhigh≥0n_{\mathrm{mid}}=N-n_{\mathrm{low}}-n_{\mathrm{high}}\geq 0. Thus feasible quotas form an integer family that trades low-budget assignments against high-budget assignments while preserving the reference mean. The quota triple is fixed before evaluation and does not use labels, policy correctness, or category-level performance. It is selected as a pre-specified operating point under the budget equation rather than by test-set accuracy. Different feasible triples correspond to different routing operating points.

Deterministic assignment.

Given (nlow,nmid,nhigh)(n_{\mathrm{low}},n_{\mathrm{mid}},n_{\mathrm{high}}), we assign routes with a high-first, low-second rule. Let argTopKi∈Sm​τi\operatorname{argTopK}_{i\in S}^{m}\tau_{i} denote the index set of the mm largest scores in SS, breaking ties deterministically with a fixed hash of the dataset index. FrameRouter first selects

H=argTopKi∈{1,…,N}nhigh​pihigh,H=\operatorname{argTopK}_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}}^{n_{\mathrm{high}}}p_{i}^{\mathrm{high}}, (5)

and assigns ri=highr_{i}=\mathrm{high} for i∈Hi\in H. It then selects the low-budget set from the remaining instances,

L=argTopKi∈{1,…,N}∖Hnlow​pilow,L=\operatorname{argTopK}_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus H}^{n_{\mathrm{low}}}p_{i}^{\mathrm{low}}, (6)

and assigns ri=lowr_{i}=\mathrm{low} for i∈Li\in L. All remaining instances are routed to the mid-budget policy. The high-first order is intentional: if an ambiguous question receives high scores for both the low- and high-policy priorities, the allocator treats the high-policy signal as the stronger constraint: wrongly compressing a high-demand question can remove needed evidence, whereas wrongly expanding a low-demand question mainly spends redundant frames. The construction guarantees, by the quota constraint, that 1N​∑i=1NBri=Bref\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}B_{r_{i}}=B_{\mathrm{ref}} holds exactly, so an accuracy gap against the uniform reference πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is not explained by a change in average compute, but by how that compute is distributed across questions. Inference then executes only the selected policy πri\pi_{r_{i}} for instance ii; the other policies in Π\Pi are not run, so there is no late selection over multiple candidate answers. The parser adds one short text-only LLM call per question, which is separate from the video-frame budget.

5 Experiments

We evaluate FrameRouter on Video-MME-v2 and three additional video understanding benchmarks, always matching the mean frame budget of the corresponding uniform mid-budget baseline.

5.1 Setup

Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate on four video understanding benchmarks: Video-MME-v2 (Fu et al., 2026), LongVideoBench (Wu et al., 2024), MVBench (Li et al., 2024), and VideoMMMU (Hu et al., 2025). Video-MME-v2 provides the most detailed protocol for our main analysis: in addition to average accuracy, it reports official group-level scores for non-linear reasoning, three difficulty levels, consistency, and coherence, and we evaluate both subtitle and no-subtitle settings. LongVideoBench is also evaluated in both subtitle settings, while MVBench and VideoMMMU are evaluated with their official accuracy metrics. Unless otherwise noted, all reported numbers follow the corresponding benchmark evaluation protocol.

Baselines.

Our controlled baseline is uniform mid-budget inference with the same Qwen3.5-397B-A17B backbone (Qwen Team, 2026). We evaluate both Instruct and Think regimes, and constrain FrameRouter to the same average visual frame budget using the frozen 48/64/96 full-video policy bank. The parser is a deterministic text-only call to the same model used by the answer-stage VLM, which receives only question/options, processes no video frames, and is capped at 160 output tokens, so its overhead is negligible compared with the heavy multimodal answer call over 48/64/96 frames and up to 1024 generated tokens. For context, we also include frontier commercial systems such as Gemini-3-Pro (Google DeepMind, 2025), GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2026), and Kimi-K2.5 (Kimi Team, 2026), together with open-source video LMMs such as Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025a), LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024), InternVL3.5 (Wang et al., 2025), and Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b).

5.2 Main results

Video-MME-v2.

Table 1 reports Video-MME-v2 results at the same 64-frame mean budget. The strongest controlled gain appears in the Think regime with subtitles: relative to the uniform Qwen3.5-397B-A17B row, FrameRouter improves average accuracy by 4.4%4.4\% and raises every group-level metric. The largest gains concentrate on the harder diagnostic axes: Level 2 improves by 7.7%7.7\%, Coherence by 5.2%5.2\%, and Non-Lin by 4.3%4.3\%. This routed Think setting is also the strongest open-source Think row in the table while using the same 64-frame mean budget. The no-subtitle and Instruct settings show the same overall direction, indicating that the benefit is not confined to a single input or decoding configuration.

Additional benchmarks.

Table 2 gives the corresponding results on MVBench, VideoMMMU, and LongVideoBench. In the Think block, FrameRouter improves over the same Qwen3.5-397B-A17B uniform row on every reported benchmark, with gains ranging from roughly 1%1\% on shorter or more saturated settings to nearly 3%3\% on LongVideoBench. The routed LongVideoBench Think result with subtitles also exceeds the listed GPT-5 reference in Table 2. The Instruct block shows a similar positive pattern, with the clearest gains appearing on VideoMMMU and LongVideoBench. Across Table 1 and Table 2, the most consistent message is that fixed-budget routing transfers across benchmarks and is especially effective on long-video and reasoning-heavy settings.

5.3 Ablation study

We ablate the two ingredients most specific to FrameRouter: direction-specific priority scores and strict-budget quota allocation. All variants use the same Think-with-subtitles setting on Video-MME-v2 and keep the mean frame budget matched to the uniform baseline.

Score channels.

Table 3 shows that both priority channels contribute useful routing signal. Using the full direction-specific parser improves average accuracy by 4.4%4.4\% over uniform inference, with larger gains on the diagnostic metrics most tied to long-video reasoning: Coherence improves by 5.2%5.2\% and Non-Lin by 4.3%4.3\%. The single-channel variants also improve substantially, indicating that each score captures a meaningful part of evidence demand; combining them yields the most consistent profile across the reported metrics.

Quota sensitivity.

Figure 3(a) sweeps the high-route quota while preserving the same mean frame budget. The selected operating point lies inside a broad high-performing region rather than at an isolated spike, and nearby quotas change the reported metrics by only a few tenths of a percent. The two curves also show that the gain is not explained by simply assigning more questions to the high-budget policy; under a fixed mean budget, useful allocation requires a balanced redistribution between compressed and promoted questions.

5.4 Router behavior analysis

Route assignments in FrameRouter are determined before answer generation from the current question alone, without access to the video, subtitles, labels, or candidate-policy outputs. We therefore use route behavior only as a post-hoc diagnostic of whether the question-only parser induces structured budget allocation under the fixed mean budget.

Figure 3(b) shows a structured allocation pattern across the official group×\timeslevel splits. The mid route remains the dominant fallback, while the low- and high-budget shares vary across question categories rather than following a uniform mixture. This supports the central premise of FrameRouter: even without observing video content or outcomes, question prompts contain enough evidence-demand signal to redistribute a fixed visual budget in a category-sensitive way.

6 Conclusion

This work studies whether a uniform per-question frame budget is the best use of a fixed average visual budget for long-video question answering. Our diagnostics on Video-MME-v2 show that nearby frame budgets help different question subsets, motivating fixed-mean frame-budget routing as a controlled test-time setting. FrameRouter instantiates this setting with a training-free question-only evidence-demand parser and a quota-constrained allocator over a frozen bank of full-video uniform policies. Across Video-MME-v2, LongVideoBench, MVBench, and VideoMMMU, the results show that matched-budget gains can be obtained by reallocating visual evidence across heterogeneous questions rather than increasing the average frame count. Budget routing is therefore a simple inference axis complementary to frame selection, token compression, and model scaling.

Appendix A Technical appendix

A.1 Additional policy-bank corrections

Section 3.2 analyzes the Think setting and shows that the low-, mid-, and high-budget policies do not form nested error sets. Here we repeat the same diagnostic for the Instruct regime to verify that budget complementarity is not specific to chain-of-thought style inference. For each official group×\timeslevel split, we compute pairwise correction matrices among the frozen full-video uniform policies. Rows denote the policy that answers a question correctly, columns denote the policy that misses it, and each mini-matrix is normalized within its split. Off-diagonal mass therefore indicates recoverable disagreement: questions that one budget handles while another budget fails.

This diagnostic is intentionally separated from the routed results. It does not use the parser, the allocator, or any learned route prediction; it only examines the frozen policy bank under different frame budgets. The Instruct setting shows that budget disagreement remains structured even without explicit reasoning traces, suggesting that frame-budget complementarity is a property of the question–evidence interaction rather than an artifact of a particular decoding style.

Figure 4 repeats the group×\timeslevel pairwise correction analysis for the Instruct regime. The off-diagonal entries remain visibly non-uniform across groups and difficulty levels, meaning that the low-, mid-, and high-budget policies recover different subsets of questions rather than forming a simple nested ordering. This mirrors the Think-setting diagnostic in the main text and supports the same design choice: FrameRouter should route among frozen full-video budget policies instead of assuming that a single uniform budget is uniformly preferable for all question types.

A.2 Parser evidence-anchor profiles

Section 5.4 reports how the final routes distribute across official group×\timeslevel splits. The diagnostic below looks at the same routed questions from the parser side. During routing, the question-only parser emits an evidence-anchor category together with its low- and high-budget priorities. These categories are not used as ground-truth annotations and are not meant to localize evidence in the video; they are self-reported parser fields that help interpret why different questions are assigned to different budget routes. We aggregate these anchor categories within each final route to check whether the route assignments correspond to coherent evidence-demand profiles.

This analysis should be read as an interpretability check rather than as an additional source of supervision. The allocator consumes only the two priority scores described in Section 4.3; the evidence-anchor field is logged for auditing and is not used to choose the route. A meaningful anchor–route association is therefore useful because it shows that the parser priorities are not arbitrary scalar scores: they are accompanied by stable, human-readable evidence profiles that align with the intended roles of the low, mid, and high routes.

Figure 5 gives a parser-side view of the realized routes. The high route is strongly enriched for temporal evidence-anchor outputs, while the low route contains more uncertain, local-visual, and subtitle-oriented profiles. The mid route remains more mixed, consistent with its role as the fallback route when neither compression nor promotion is strongly preferred. These anchors are not human annotations and do not imply temporal localization, but they help verify that the question-only parser induces interpretable route structure rather than an arbitrary budget mixture.

A.3 Implementation details

This section summarizes implementation details of our method. The default configuration matches the main Video-MME-v2 Think-with-subtitles setting unless otherwise specified.

Hyperparameters.

FrameRouter uses a three-policy full-video uniform bank with low, mid, and high budgets set to 48, 64, and 96 frames, respectively. For the 48/64/96 bank this gives twice as many low routes as high routes. Parser and answer calls use temperature 0.00.0 by default. The parser response length is 160 tokens, while the answer response length is 1024 tokens.

Deterministic allocation and parsing.

The parser returns priority_48, priority_96, confidence, evidence_anchor, and a short rationale. Scores are clamped to [0,1][0,1], and malformed or missing scores default to conservative mid-range values. The allocator first selects the high route by descending priority_96, then selects the low route from the remaining questions by descending priority_48; all remaining questions use the mid route. Ties are broken by a deterministic hash of the dataset index, and the code raises an error if the allocated mean frame count differs from the mid-budget target. The answer stage then runs only the selected route for each question, using uniform sampling and the baseline Video-MME-v2 prompt layout inherited from the evaluation script.

Evidence-demand priority parser prompt.

The released parser prompt is presented below. The prompt explicitly states the information boundary of the router, the fixed-mean budget setting, the semantics of the two priority scores, and the required JSON output format.

You are a text-only priority router for long-video multiple-choice QA.You cannot see the video and you do not know the answer. Use only the currentquestion and answer options. Do not answer the question. Do not use labels,sibling questions, other videos, or dataset statistics.A strict solver will keep the average budget fixed at 64 frames:- a small top group by priority_96 will use 96 frames;- twice as many questions by priority_48 will use 48 frames;- all remaining questions will use the default 64 frames.Your job is to output the two final ranking priorities directly. Do not output aweighted formula; do not choose the number of questions assigned to each budget.priority_48 should be high only when reducing 64f to 48f is likely safe:- the decisive evidence is local, static, repeated, or easy to locate;- 64f looks more than sufficient from the question/options;- the question is anchored by a clear subtitle/dialogue/text/object cue;- no broad temporal coverage, counting, order tracking, or subtle multi-scene comparison is needed.priority_96 should be high only when extra frames are likely useful:- subtitle/dialogue/text anchoring is weak or absent;- the decisive visual evidence is hard to localize from text alone;- broad temporal coverage, counting, event order, changes, or repeated actions are central;- the options require fine visual discrimination across moments.Important calibration:- Most questions should remain 64f, so both priorities should often be modest.- Do not make priority_96 high merely because the question seems hard; extra frames only help when the missing evidence is temporal/visual coverage.- Do not make priority_48 high for OCR, tiny text, rare brief details, or fine visual distinctions even if the evidence is local.- If unsure, set both priorities near 0.40-0.55 and confidence below 0.60.Return compact JSON only:{"policy": "DEFAULT_64F","priority_48": 0.00,"priority_96": 0.00,"confidence": 0.00,"evidence_anchor": "subtitle|visual_local|visual_broad|temporal|mixed|uncertain","rationale": "<=10 words"}Question:{question}Options:{options}

Answer-stage prompts.

The answer stage uses the baseline Video-MME-v2 prompt layout from the official evaluation script.

A.4 Code release

The code implementation of FrameRouter is publicly available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter. The code is organized to match the method contract in Section 4.2: the router first reads only the current question and its answer options, assigns one frame budget, and then runs exactly one selected full-video uniform policy. It does not inspect video frames, subtitles, labels, sibling questions, other videos, or any candidate-policy outputs before route assignment. The released pipeline therefore implements the deployable path used in the paper rather than a post-hoc selector that runs multiple answer policies and chooses among their outputs.

Module structure.

The entry point is run_framerouter.py, with command-line arguments defined in framerouter/cli.py. Runtime and frame-budget settings are kept in framerouter/config.py. The question-only routing prompt is in framerouter/router_prompt.py, while framerouter/router.py performs the parser call, JSON extraction, and parser TSV normalization. The deterministic fixed-mean budget assignment is implemented in framerouter/allocation.py. After allocation, framerouter/policy.py runs the selected 48/64/96-frame Video-MME-v2 inference policy, and framerouter/scoring.py wraps Video-MME-v2 scoring. The end-to-end orchestration lives in framerouter/pipeline.py; run_videommev2.sh provides an example command for the main Video-MME-v2 setting.

current question/options -> framerouter.router # evidence-demand scores -> framerouter.allocation # fixed-mean budget assignment -> framerouter.policy # selected full-video policy only -> framerouter.scoring # Video-MME-v2 metrics

Environment and execution.

The paper experiments were run on an 8×\timesNVIDIA H200 server using vLLM with the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API and a Python 3.10+ client. The inputs are Video-MME-v2 parquet metadata, extracted video files, and subtitle JSONL files. Frames may be transported as base64-encoded JPEGs or through local media paths supported by the inference server. The implementation is otherwise model-server agnostic as long as the server accepts OpenAI-compatible multimodal chat-completions requests.

A typical run first starts a vLLM server:

python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model <MODEL_PATH_OR_NAME> \ --served-model-name qwen35-think \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --port 8000 \ --trust-remote-code

FrameRouter can then be launched with the provided script:

bash run_videommev2.sh

For quick verification, the release also supports a small smoke test via --limit and an allocation-only mode via --only-allocate when an existing parser TSV is available.

Outputs.

The script writes parser.tsv for question-only parser scores, routes.tsv for route assignments and allocated frame counts, predictions.tsv for selected-policy predictions and raw responses, predictions_scored.tsv for scored question-level outputs, and predictions_rating.json for aggregate Video-MME-v2 metrics.
